_about: The wrath hub (plan 7.6f, third round). The card 'wrath' is named 'anger' and stands on the Hebrew אַף and the Greek θυμός; the hub adds the rest of the family the English renders wrath, anger, fury and indignation: the Greek ὀργή (the New Testament's usual word: Rom 1:18, Eph 2:3), the Hebrew חֵמָה, חָרוֹן, זַעַם, קֶצֶף and עֶבְרָה, the Aramaic חֱמָא of Daniel, and the verbs of being angry (חָרָה 'burn, be angry', אָנַף, קָצַף, זָעַם, ὀργίζω, θυμόω). The nouns are sorted by the words standing beside them in the verse or the clause (in_verse, in_clause) and by the text's own phrase (with: 'the anger of the LORD'); the verbs, whose frames the graph holds for only about three in four, are sorted by hand (the divine persons by hand): the verses where the text names God angry, and the verses where a person is. The contested points -- what turns wrath away (what is called propitiation, and expiation), 'children of wrath', whether God's wrath is a personal response or what sin brings with it, an oath sworn in anger -- are set side by side, the words of each verse shown, each with a note that the page takes no side. Human anger is its own rows and never the same row as God's. Built by tools/concepts/hub_build.py into out/concept-hubs/wrath.json.

titles.noun: What the text says of wrath and anger
titles.verb: Who is angry, and with whom

_words_why: The card's two (אַף 'anger', literally the nostril that flares; θυμός) and the others the English renders the same way and that the Greek Old Testament pairs with them: ὀργή renders אַף, חָרוֹן, זַעַם, קֶצֶף and עֶבְרָה; חֵמָה (heat, rage) is the commonest Hebrew word after אַף. The Aramaic חֱמָא is Daniel's 'rage' (Dan 2:12; 3:13, 19). The verbs: חָרָה 'burn' is said of anger ('his anger burned'), אָנַף and קָצַף 'be angry', זָעַם 'be indignant', ὀργίζω 'make angry, be angry', θυμόω 'be furious' (Herod, Matt 2:16). The hub never says the Hebrew and the Greek are one word: every verse names the word it stands on. The twin card 'anger' (id anger) stands on exactly the same two words, אַף and θυμός: its words belong here, in the rows, and not under the other words, since they are the same words and not words the English also calls anger; see the report for how the two cards should be handled. The Hebrew words for 'provoke to anger' (כָּעַס), 'rage' (זַעַף, רֹגֶז, רָגַז) and 'keep, harbor' (נָטַר) are different words and are named apart under the other words.
_sense_why: Measured on MACULA's gloss in each verse (2026-10-25, build 1). חֵמָה is also 'venom, poison' (Deut 32:24, 33; Job 6:4; Ps 58:4, 140:3), which the gloss rule leaves out, and 'heat' of wine (Hos 7:5, dropped by hand). אַף is also 'nose', 'nostrils' and 'face' ('bowed with his face to the ground'): 52 verses drop out as another sense. חָרָה is 'burn' also of the scorched inhabitants of the earth (Isa 24:6, dropped by hand), of Nehemiah's zeal (Neh 3:20) and of 'fret' (Ps 37:1): not the sense. עֶבְרָה is 'insolence' at Isa 16:6 and Jer 48:30 and 'arrogant' at Prov 21:24: those drop out. זָעַם is 'denounce, curse' at Num 23:7-8 and Prov 22:14: 4 verses drop out.

Hos.7.5.why: חֵמָה is the 'heat' of wine that inflames the princes, not anger

Isa.24.6.why: חָרָה here is 'scorched' (the inhabitants of the earth are burned), not anger

others._why: Different words the English also renders anger, wrath or fury, named apart with their verses and never handed over as the same word (as love names φιλέω). כָּעַס and כַּעַס are 'provoke to anger' and 'vexation': what Israel does to the LORD by idols, not the LORD's own anger. παροργίζω and παροργισμός are Paul's 'provoke to anger' (Rom 10:19; Eph 4:26). זַעַף and רֹגֶז are 'rage'; נָטַר is 'keep, harbor' (Ps 103:9). רָגַז is 'be agitated, tremble, be angry' (Ps 4:4, which Eph 4:26 quotes; added by hand 2026-10-25 after the panel).
others.title: Other words translated “anger”, “wrath”, “fury”

h3707.note: כָּעַס means to vex, provoke to anger: what Israel does to the LORD with idols (Deut 32:16, 1 Kgs 14:9). A different word from אַף; the page does not make the two one.

h7264.note: רָגַז means to be agitated, to tremble, to be angry. Eph 4:26 (“Be angry, yet do not sin”) quotes this verse. A different word from אַף; the page does not make the two one.

_review: Not yet reviewed by Doug. Written against the brief for the third round of hubs (2026-10-25). 16-verse check on build 3: 14 showed their row's label; two did not and were fixed (Job 19:29 under 'Anger and sin': the Berean prints עָוֺן as 'punishment', taken out; Deut 9:22 under 'God angry': the Berean prints 'provoke', moved to 'Every other use'). Four other corrections from reading the verbs: 1 Sam 15:11 (Berean 'distressed') left out, Gen 18:30 and 18:32 moved from 'a person angry' to 'God angry'. The eleven-seat panel then read it (see _review_2026_10_25 for what was applied, held and declined). Contested points for the editor: 'Wrath turned aside' and 'The atoning sacrifice' (propitiation and expiation), 'Children of wrath, vessels of wrath', the note on 'The anger of the LORD, the wrath of God' (a personal response, or what sin brings), 'The coming wrath, and being saved from it' (when, and who passes through it), 'An oath sworn in anger', 'Asked of God against enemies' (hard verses kept), 'Jesus and wrath', and the verb rows (the divine persons by hand; Ps 2:12 left out of both).

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Split 'The day of wrath; wrath to come, and shelter from it' in two: the Old Testament verses (Zeph 1:15, 1:18, 2:2-3; Lam 1:12, 2:1, 2:21-22; Isa 13:13, 26:20; Job 14:13, 20:28, 21:30; Ps 110:5; Prov 11:4; Ezek 7:19, 22:24) under 'The day of wrath, the day of His anger' with no 'to come' wording and Old Testament examples first; the New Testament verses under 'The coming wrath, and being saved from it' with a label quote taken from Matt 3:7
_review_2026_10_25.why: Both halves asked for it; the prophets' day is described as a day already fallen or proverbial, and the heading read the New Testament's frame back onto them. The page does not say when any of these days falls.

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Take Luke 21:23 and 1 Thess 2:16 out of the 'wrath to come' row (they say wrath is 'against this people' and 'has come upon them'); 1 Thess 2:16 falls to 'Every other use', Luke 21:23 stays in 'Anger against Israel, Judah and Jerusalem' but no longer leads it; a sentence in the new row's note names the two
_review_2026_10_25.why: The verb tense differs from the verses of the wrath to come; panel a kept Luke 21:23 in the row but did not argue for it. 1 Thess 2:16 was not added to the Israel row, so the page does not set a verse about 'them' under a heading about a people.

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Relabel and split 'What stands between wrath and the people': 'Wrath turned aside' (Exod 32:12, Num 16:46, Num 25:11, Ps 106:23, Jer 18:20, Dan 9:16, Rom 5:9) and a short row 'The atoning sacrifice' (Rom 3:25, Heb 2:17, 1 John 2:2, 1 John 4:10) that keeps the propitiation / expiation note; the label no longer says what the sacrifice does
_review_2026_10_25.why: The old heading asserted the propitiation reading its own note says is open, over four verses with no wrath word. Rom 5:9 has the wrath word and 'His blood' and stays in this row and in the coming-wrath row; panel a would also have put it in the atoning row, but its Berean words are 'saved from wrath through Him', not 'atoning sacrifice', so it is not set there.

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Keep Ps 78:38 in the 'turned aside' row (panel a's list)
_review_2026_10_25.why: Ps 78:38 has the LORD Himself forgiving and holding back His anger, with no intercessor, priest or zealous man; panel b was right that it does not show the label. It stays in 'Anger and mercy' and 'Anger turned away'.

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Replace the 'Children of wrath' note: begin with what Eph 2:3 says (the Berean's own sentence), say readers part on what 'by nature' says and where the condition comes from, add that traditions answer this differently within themselves, and add that in Rom 9:22 readers part on who prepared the vessels
_review_2026_10_25.why: The old note named two doctrinal answers as if they were the only two and left out Rom 9:22. The new note names none of the answers.

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Rom 13:4-5: shorten the label of 'Wrath and judgment, vengeance' and carry the ruler in the note with the Berean's words ('an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer', 'to avoid punishment'), saying the Greek word in both is ὀργή; Rom 13:4 no longer leads the row
_review_2026_10_25.why: The old label and note quoted a translation other than the Berean (checked: 13:4 reads 'an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer'). Panel b's shorter label was taken over panel a's longer one, since a label should not carry a detail of two verses out of 21.

_review_2026_10_25.fix: 'Anger that burns': replace Gen 30:2 among the four examples with Isa 30:30 (Berean: 'a flame of consuming fire')
_review_2026_10_25.why: Gen 30:2 reads 'Jacob became angry with Rachel' in the Berean; the Hebrew verb for burning is not visible in the English. It stays in the row (the Hebrew is חָרָה) but is no longer an example.

_review_2026_10_25.fix: A note on both 'Anger that burns' and 'Anger turned away': 'These rows hold both the LORD's anger and people's; each verse shows whose.'
_review_2026_10_25.why: Both rows hold God's and a person's anger by rule; the verses show whose, and the note says so.

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Remove Jer 4:4 from 'Anger turned away' (not_verses)

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Move Prov 19:11, 22:24, 29:22 out of 'Anger and sin, idols, unfaithfulness' (they are sayings on a hot-tempered person and already stand in 'A person's anger')

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Hab 3:2: give the example a word chip for רֹגֶז
_review_2026_10_25.why: A row can show a chip only for the hub's own words, and רֹגֶז (h7267) is deliberately one of the other words, where Hab 3:2 is already listed. Instead the 'Cries' row's note now names the word.

rows.label: The anger of the LORD, the wrath of God
rows.note: The text's own phrase, kept as written. Rom 1:18 reads "The wrath of God is being revealed"; the verses after it read "God gave them over" (1:24, 26) and "He gave them up" (1:28), the same Greek verb each time, and have no word for wrath. Readers part on what the wrath of God is -- God's own response to evil, or what sin brings with it -- and the page takes no side.

rows.label: Slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion; anger beside mercy, compassion, favor, forgiveness

not_verses.Prov.14.29: a saying on a person who is slow to anger, not the LORD's patience; it stands in 'A person's anger'
not_verses.Prov.15.18: a saying on a hot-tempered man and one who is slow to anger; it stands in 'A person's anger'
not_verses.Prov.16.32: a saying on a person who is slow to anger; it stands in 'A person's anger'
not_verses.Jas.1.19: 'slow to anger' said of a person; it stands in the letters' row on a person's anger

rows.note: The words of Exod 34:6 come back in Num 14:18, Neh 9:17, Ps 86:15, 103:8, 145:8, Joel 2:13 and Jonah 4:2; in Jonah 4:2 Jonah says them to the LORD after his own anger (Jonah 4:1, 4, under "A person angry"). The text sets the anger beside mercy in its own pairs, and the page does not say how they are reconciled.
rows._why: merged 2026-10-25 from 'Slow to anger; patience beside wrath' and 'Anger and mercy, compassion, favor, forgiveness': eight verses stood in both and the formula was cut in two. The sayings on a person's patience are taken out by hand.

rows.label: The day of wrath, the day of His anger: “That day will be a day of wrath”, “in the day of His anger”
rows.note: The verses are set as they stand, in the prophets' and poets' own words. The page does not say when any of these days falls.
rows._why: split 2026-10-25 from 'The day of wrath; wrath to come, and shelter from it': the Old Testament verses by hand, the same 17 the rule had found, so none is lost and none gets a New Testament heading

rows.label: The coming wrath, and being saved from it: “flee from the coming wrath”, “saved from wrath”, “not appointed us to suffer wrath”
rows.note: Where Christian traditions part on when the coming wrath comes and who passes through it, the page takes no side; it sets the verses as they stand. Two verses that speak of wrath as already come or as against a people, 1 Thess 2:16 ("the utmost wrath has come upon them") and Luke 21:23 ("wrath against this people"), are not set here.
rows._why: split 2026-10-25: the New Testament verses of the wrath to come and of being saved from it, by hand

rows.label: Wrath poured out; the cup of wrath, the winepress of wrath
rows._why: the rule is the verb 'pour out' with the anger as its object; the cup and winepress verses are named by hand because they are the same picture in other verbs (drink, tread). Rev 14:8 and 18:3 ('the wine of the passion of her immorality') are not here: the Berean prints θυμός as 'passion' there.

rows.label: Anger that burns, is kindled, flares like fire
rows.note: These rows hold both the LORD's anger and people's; each verse shows whose.

rows.label: Anger turned away, or not turned away; restrained, quenched, spent

not_verses.Isa.14.6: 'relentless' (חָשַׂךְ): the oppressor's rage that was not held back, not anger turned away
not_verses.Amos.1.11: 'revoke' is said of the punishment, not of anger turned away
not_verses.2Chr.25.10: 'returned home' (שׁוּב): the soldiers went home in anger
not_verses.Isa.66.15: 'to execute His anger' (שׁוּב hiphil 'render'), not turning away
not_verses.Jer.32.31: 'remove it from My presence' (סוּר) is said of the city, not of anger
not_verses.Jer.4.4: 'remove' (סוּר) is said of the foreskins of the heart, not of the anger; the verse says the wrath will break out like fire

rows.note: These rows hold both the LORD's anger and people's; each verse shows whose.
rows._why: the rule is the turning-away verb in the same clause as the anger; 'not turned away' (Isa 5:25; 9:12) is the same clause negated and is kept, since the text says it of the same anger. Hos 11:9, Isa 48:9 and Ezek 5:13, 6:12, 13:15, 16:42, 24:13 ('I will not carry out My fierce anger'; 'for My name's sake I delay My wrath'; 'when My anger is spent') are named by hand: their verbs are 'carry out', 'delay', 'spend'.

rows.label: Anger and sin, idols, unfaithfulness

not_verses.Ps.27.9: עָזַב is 'forsake me not', the psalmist's plea, not the people's unfaithfulness
not_verses.Job.18.4: עָזַב is 'the earth be forsaken', not unfaithfulness
not_verses.Job.19.29: עָוֺן is printed 'punishment' (wrath brings punishment by the sword); the Berean's verse names no sin
not_verses.Ps.37.8: עָזַב is 'forsake wrath' (abandon anger), not unfaithfulness
not_verses.Nah.1.2: בַּעַל is 'master of wrath' (בַּעַל חֵמָה), not Baal
not_verses.Dan.8.6: בַּעַל is 'with the two horns' (בַּעַל הַקְּרָנַיִם), not Baal
not_verses.Jer.25.38: עָזַב is the lion who 'has left his lair'
not_verses.Prov.19.11: a saying on a person's patience, not God's anger at sin; it stands in 'A person's anger'
not_verses.Prov.22.24: a saying on a hot-tempered person, not God's anger at sin; it stands in 'A person's anger'
not_verses.Prov.29.22: a saying on an angry man, not God's anger at sin; it stands in 'A person's anger'

rows.label: Anger against the nations, enemies and the wicked

not_verses.Rev.14.8: the Berean prints θυμός as 'the passion of her immorality': not wrath against the nations
not_verses.Rev.18.3: the Berean prints θυμός as 'the passion of her immorality': not wrath against the nations
not_verses.Isa.14.6: the rage of the tyrant king of Babylon that struck the peoples, not God's anger against them; it stands in 'Anger in the stories, and a king's wrath'
not_verses.Prov.11.23: 'the hope of the wicked brings wrath': no nation or enemy in view

rows.label: Anger against Israel, Judah and Jerusalem
rows.note: In 2 Kgs 3:27 the verse does not say whose wrath it is.

rows.label: Anger and the law, the covenant, the commandments, “this book”

not_verses.Job.14.13: חֹק is 'a set time' (appoint me a time), not a statute
not_verses.Zeph.2.2: חֹק is 'the decree' that takes effect, not the law

rows.note: In Deut 29:20, 2 Chr 34:21 and 2 Kgs 22:13 the Berean reads "every curse written in this book", "all that is written in this book" and "the words of this book"; the English does not say "law" or "covenant" there.
rows._why: Deut 29:20, 2 Chr 34:21 and 2 Kgs 22:13 added by hand after the panel (the covenant's own curse as the frame of wrath: Josiah finds the book)

rows.label: Wrath and judgment, vengeance
rows.note: Rom 12:19 reads "leave room for God's wrath" and quotes "Vengeance is Mine". Of the governing authority Rom 13:4 reads "an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer" and 13:5 "to avoid punishment"; the Greek word in both is ὀργή, wrath. The page sets the words and does not say more.

rows.label: An oath sworn in anger: that generation shall not enter the land; “they shall never enter My rest”
rows.note: Hebrews 3:7-4:11 takes up Psalm 95 and speaks of the rest God promised and the people did not enter. Readers take "My rest" differently: the land, God's own rest, or the rest of the believer. The page sets the verses and takes no side.

rows.label: Cries to the LORD about His anger: “do not rebuke me in Your anger”, “How long?”, “In Your wrath, remember mercy”
rows.note: In Hab 3:2 the Hebrew word for "wrath" is רֹגֶז, which is one of the other words, listed below.

rows.label: Asked of God against enemies: “consume them in wrath”, “Pour out Your wrath on the nations”
rows._why: by hand, hard verses kept (rule 7): the prayers that ask the wrath of God on those who oppose the speaker. Jer 18:23 asks that their iniquity not be forgiven and that they be overthrown 'in the time of Your anger'.

rows.label: The rod and the weapons of His wrath: Assyria, the land of the Chaldeans, an army from faraway lands, a stormy wind
rows._why: by hand: the verses where the text names what carries the wrath out -- 'the rod of My anger' (Isa 10:5), 'the weapons of His wrath' (Isa 13:5; Jer 50:25), 'the rod of His wrath' (Lam 3:1), 'a stormy wind in My wrath' (Ezek 13:13). Isa 10:6 and Isa 13:3 are the next verses of the same words. Relabelled 2026-10-25 after the panel: Jer 50:25 names the land of the Chaldeans, Isa 13:5 'faraway lands', and only Isa 10:5 names Assyria.

rows.label: Wrath turned aside: Moses stands in the breach, Aaron's censer, Phinehas' zeal, Jeremiah's and Daniel's prayer; “saved from wrath through Him”
rows.note: The verses are set as they stand. Rom 5:9 is the one New Testament verse here; the page does not say how it relates to the others.
rows._why: split 2026-10-25 from 'What stands between wrath and the people': the verses where the text itself has wrath turned aside or held back, each with its wrath word. Ps 78:38 is not here (the LORD Himself holds back; no one stands between). The four 'atoning sacrifice' verses are in the next row.

rows.label: The atoning sacrifice: the Berean's “atoning sacrifice” and “make atonement”
rows.note: The Berean prints the Greek ἱλαστήριον, ἱλασμός and ἱλάσκομαι as "atoning sacrifice" and "make atonement" (Rom 3:25; 1 John 2:2, 4:10; Heb 2:17), and none of those four verses has a word for wrath. Readers part on what the word says: a sacrifice that turns God's wrath aside (propitiation), one that removes sin (expiation), or both. The page sets the words and takes no side.
rows._why: split 2026-10-25: the four verses with no wrath word, under a label of the Berean's own words, so the propitiation / expiation question stays in the note and not in a heading

rows.label: Children of wrath, vessels of wrath
rows.note: Eph 2:3 reads "All of us also lived among them at one time, fulfilling the cravings of our flesh and indulging its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature children of wrath" (the Greek for "by nature" is φύσει). Readers part on what "by nature" says and where the condition comes from, and traditions answer this differently within themselves. In Rom 9:22 readers part on who prepared the vessels for destruction, God or those who are in them. The page takes no side.

rows.label: Jesus and wrath: “the wrath of the Lamb”, “who rescues us from the coming wrath”, “looked around at them with anger”
A person's anger: “A gentle answer turns away wrath”, “refrain from anger”, “Cursed be their anger”

What Jesus and the letters say of a person's anger: “anyone who is angry with his brother”, “Be angry, yet do not sin”, “man's anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires”, “Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger”
rows.note: Eph 4:26 quotes Psalm 4:4, which is listed below with the other words.

rows.label: Anger in the stories, and a king's wrath: a brother, a master, a king, Haman, a crowd, the devil
Every other use
rows.note: Among them: the LORD's own words ("My anger", "My wrath") and the prophets' and psalmists' words of His anger, where the verse names neither the LORD nor a companion word of the rows above (Exod 15:7; Isa 13:9; Jer 21:5; Ezek 7:12, 25:14; Zech 1:2); Job's and his friends' speeches (Job 4:9; 9:5; 16:9; 21:17); Moses' fear of the anger (Deut 9:19); "the wrath of man shall praise You" (Ps 76:10); "the time of wrath is completed" (Dan 11:36); "the utmost wrath has come upon them" (1 Thess 2:16). Rev 14:8 and 18:3 read "the wine of the passion of her immorality": the Greek θυμός, which the Berean prints "passion" there and "wrath" in 14:10.

rows.label: God angry: “the LORD was angry with you”, “the anger of the LORD burned against”, “Will You be angry forever?”
rows.note: Not in this row, by choice: Ps 2:12 ("lest He be angry"), where readers take differently whom "He" means and the page does not choose; Deut 9:22 ("You continued to provoke the LORD"), the Hebrew verb קָצַף in its causing form, "provoke to wrath", which the Berean prints only as "provoke"; and 1 Sam 15:11, which reads "Samuel was distressed" in the Berean where the Hebrew verb is חָרָה, "burned, became angry" (a finding; the verse is in no row because its English does not show the label).
rows._why: by hand (divine persons by hand): each verse names the LORD or God as the one angry (or makes Him so, as 'you provoked the LORD to wrath'), or addresses Him ('Will You be angry with us forever?', Ps 85:5; 'Do not let Your anger burn against me', Judg 6:39). The frames hold the verb for only about three in four of these verses (Num 11:1, 11:10, 11:33, 22:22 and Deut 6:15, 7:4, 11:17 have none), so a rule on the frames would have missed them. Ps 2:12 ('lest He be angry') is in no row: whom 'He' means is a reading the page does not make (the verb catch-all was dropped after the panel, 2026-10-25; the verse is under More and named in the note). Gen 18:30 and 18:32 ('May the Lord not be angry') are Abraham's plea and are here, not under a person angry. Deut 9:22 is in no row: the Berean prints 'provoke', not 'anger' (16-verse check, build 3).

rows.label: A person angry: Cain, Jacob, Moses, Saul, David, Naaman, Jonah, the elder brother, a king in a parable; “Why are you angry?”
rows._why: by hand: the verses where the verb is said of a person, a king, a master, the nations or the dragon. The frames lack Gen 4:5-6 (Cain), Gen 18:30, 34:7, 45:5, 1 Sam 15:11, 18:8, 2 Sam 3:8, 6:8, 13:21, 19:42, Neh 5:6 and Jonah 4:1, 4, 9. Matt 18:34 and 22:7 are the master and the king of Jesus' parables. Isa 24:6 is not here: the verb is 'scorched'.
